title: Fame without rank, wealth or country
source_text: Ἀνθρώποις μὲν γὰρ συμβάλλεται πρὸς τὸ γενέσθαι τινὰ αὐτῶν διάσημον καὶ ἔνδοξον καὶ τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ διαβόητον γένος, ὅταν οἱ γονεῖς ἐν ὑπεροχῇ καὶ προαγωγῇ τυγχάνωσι. καὶ πλοῦτος τῶν ἀναθρεψαμένων καὶ δυνηθέντων ἀναλῶσαι εἰς παίδευσιν τοῦ υἱοῦ καὶ πατρὶς μεγάλη τις οὖσα καὶ ἐπίσημος. ὅταν δὲ πάντα τὰ τούτοις ἐναντία ἔχων τις δυνηθῇ ὑπερκύψας τὰ ἐμποδίζοντα αὐτὸν γνωσθῆναι καὶ σεῖσαι τοὺς περὶ αὐτοῦ ἀκούοντας καὶ γενέσθαι ἐμφανὴς καὶ δῆλος οἰκουμένῃ ὅλῃ, τὰ ἀνόμοια λεγούσῃ περὶ αὐτοῦ, πῶς οὐ θανμαστέον τὴν τοιαύτην φύσιν αὐτόθεν μὲν ὡς μεγαλοφυῆ καὶ μεγάλοις ἐπιβάλλουσαν πράγμασι καὶ ἔχουσαν παῤῥησίαν οὐκ εὐκαταφρόνητον; εἰ δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ πλεῖον ἐξετάζοι τις τὰ κατὰ τὸν τοιοῦτον. πῶς οὐκ ἂν ζητήσαι, τίνα τρόπον ἐν εὐτελείᾳ καὶ πενίᾳ ἀνατεθραμμένος καὶ μηδεμίαν ἐγκύκλιον παιδείαν παιδευθεὶς μηδὲ μαθὼν λόγους καὶ δόγματα, ἀφ᾿ ὧν κἂν πιθανὸς γενέσθαι ἐδύνατο ὁμιλεῖν ὄχλοις καὶ δημαγωγεῖν καὶ ἐπάγεσθαι ἀκροατὰς πλείονας, ἐπιδίδωσιν ἑαυτὸν διδασκαλίᾳ καινῶν δογμάτων, ἐπεισάγων τῷ γένει τῶν ἀνθρώπων λόγον τά τε Ἰουδαίων ἔθη καταλύοντα μετὰ τοῦ σεμνοποιεῖν αὐτῶν τοὺς προφήτας καὶ τοὺς Ἑλλήνων νόμους μάλιστα περὶ τοῦ θείου καθαιροῦντα; πῶς δ᾿ ἂν ὁ τοιοῦτος καὶ οὕτως ἀνατεθραμμένος καὶ μηδὲν (ὡς καὶ οἱ κακολογοῦντες αὐτὸν ὁμολογοῦσι) σεμνὸν παρὰ ἀνθρώπου μαθὼν τοιαῦτα περὶ κρίσεως θεοῦ καὶ κολάσεων μὲν τῶν κατὰ τῆς κακίας τιμῶν δὲ τῶν ὑπὲρ τοῦ καλοῦ λέγειν ἐδύνατο οὐκ εὐκαταφρονήτως, ὥστ᾿ οὐ μόνον ἀγροίκους καὶ ἰδιώτας ἄγεσθαι ὑπὸ τῶν λεγομένων ἀλλὰ καὶ οὐκ ὀλίγους τῶν συνετωτέρων καὶ δυναμένων ἐνορᾶν ἀποκρύψει τῶν εὐτελεστέρων νομιζομένων ἀπαγγέλλεσθαι, περιεχούσῃ τι. ὡς ἔστιν εἰπεῖν. ἔνδον ἀποῤῥητότερον; ὁ μὲν οὖν παρὰ τῷ Πλάτωνι Σερίφιος ὀνειδίζων τῷ Θεμιστοκλεῖ, διαβοήτῳ γεγενημένῳ ἐπὶ τῇ στρατηγίᾳ, ὡς οὐκ ἐκ τοῦ ἰδίου ἤθους τὸ ἔνδοξον ἀνειληφότι ἀλλ᾿ ἐκ τοῦ εὐτυχηκέναι πατρίδος τῆς ἐν ὅλῃ Ἑλλάδι ἐπισημοτάτης. ἀκήκοεν ἀπὸ εὐγνωμονοῦντος Θεμιστοκλέους καὶ ὁρῶντος ὅτι συνεβάλετο αὐτῷ πρὸς τὸ ἔνδοξον καὶ ἡ πατρὶς, ὅτι „οὔτ᾿ ἂν ἐγὼ Σερίφιος ὢν οὕτως ἔνδοξος ἐγεγόνειν, οὔτε σὺ Ἀθηναῖος εὐτυχήσας γενέσθαι ἐγένου ἂν Θεμιστοκλῆς“· ὁ δ᾿ ἡμέτερος Ἰησοῦς καὶ ὀνειδιζόμενος ὡς ἐκ κώμης γεγονὼς καὶ ταύτης οὐχ Ἑλλαδικῆς οὐδέ τινος ἔθνους ἔθνους ὄντος παρὰ τοῖς πολλοῖς ἐν προαγωγῇ, δυσφημούμενος δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ τῷ πενιχρᾶς καὶ χερνήτιδος υἱὸς εἶναι καὶ διὰ πενίαν καταλιπὼν τὴν πατρίδα ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ μισθαρνῆσαι. καὶ οἱονεὶ πρὸς τὸ ληφθὲν παράδειγμα οὐ μόνον Σερίφιος γεγονὼς καὶ ἀπὸ ἐλαχίστης καὶ ἀσημοτάτης νήσου ἀλλὰ καὶ Σεριφίων, ὡς ἔστιν εἰπεῖν, ὁ ἀγεννέστατος, δεδύνηται σεῖσαι τὴν πᾶσαν ἀνθρώπων οἰκουμένην οὐ μόνον ὑπὲρ Θεμιστοκλέα τὸν Ἀθηναῖον ἀλλὰ καὶ ὑπὲρ Πυθαγόραν καὶ Πλάτωνα καί τινας ἄλλους τῶν ὁποιποτοῦν τῆς οἰκουμένης σοφῶν ἢ βασιλέων ἢ στρατηγῶν.
pass_a_gloss: For among men, toward one of them becoming distinguished (διάσημος) and glorious (ἔνδοξος) and his name noised about (διαβόητος), lineage (γένος) contributes (συμβάλλεται), when the parents are in eminence (ὑπεροχή) and advancement (προαγωγή); and wealth (πλοῦτος) of those who reared him and could spend on the son's education (παίδευσις); and a fatherland (πατρίς) being great and notable (ἐπίσημος). But when one having all the opposites can, peering over/rising above (ὑπερκύπτω) the things hindering him from being known, shake (σείω) those hearing about him and become manifest (ἐμφανής) and evident to the whole world, which says unlike/discordant things (ἀνόμοια) about him, how is such a nature not to be wondered at - at once (αὐτόθεν) as great-natured (μεγαλοφυής), setting upon great matters, and having a frankness/boldness (παρρησία) not easily despised? And if one examined further the affairs of such a man, how would he not inquire how, reared in cheapness (εὐτέλεια) and poverty, educated in no general education (ἐγκύκλιος παιδεία), nor having learned arguments and doctrines (δόγματα) by which he could have become persuasive (πιθανός) to address crowds (ὄχλοι), lead the people (δημαγωγέω) and draw more hearers, he gives himself to teaching of new doctrines (καινὰ δόγματα), introducing to the human race a word that both dissolves (καταλύω) the customs (ἔθη) of the Jews while revering (σεμνοποιέω) their prophets, and pulls down (καθαιρέω) the laws (νόμοι) of the Greeks especially about the divine (τὸ θεῖον)? And how could such a one, so reared, having learned nothing venerable (σεμνόν) from a man (as even his revilers agree), say such things not contemptibly about God's judgment (κρίσις θεοῦ), and punishments (κολάσεις) against vice (κακία) and honours (τιμαί) for the good, that not only rustics and unlearned are led by what is said but also not a few of the more intelligent, able to see into (ἐνοράω) the concealment (ἀπόκρυψις) of things thought to be told in cheaper terms, [a concealment] containing, so to say, something more secret (ἀπορρητότερον) within? The Seriphian in Plato, reproaching Themistocles, famed for generalship (στρατηγία), as having taken up his glory not from his own character (ἦθος) but from having had the good fortune (εὐτυχέω) of the most notable fatherland in all Greece, heard from Themistocles, who was fair-minded (εὐγνωμονέω) and saw that the fatherland too contributed to his glory: 'Neither would I, being a Seriphian, have become so glorious, nor would you, having had the luck to be born an Athenian, have become Themistocles.' But our Jesus, reproached as having come from a village, and that not Greek, nor of any nation in esteem with the many, defamed (δυσφημέω) as son of a poor hand-working woman and as having left his fatherland through poverty to work for wages in Egypt, and, as it were by the example taken, not only a Seriphian from the smallest and most obscure island but, so to say, the most ignoble (ἀγεννέστατος) of Seriphians, has been able to shake the whole inhabited world of men, beyond (ὑπέρ) not only Themistocles the Athenian but also Pythagoras and Plato and any others of the wise, or kings, or generals of the world anywhere.
pass_b_english: Among human beings, what helps a man become distinguished and famous, with his name spoken of everywhere, is birth, when his parents happen to be eminent and of high standing; the wealth of those who raised him and could afford to spend on their son’s education; and a fatherland that is great and renowned. But when someone who has everything opposite to these is able to rise above all that keeps him from becoming known, to stir those who hear of him, and to become conspicuous and well known to the whole world, a world that says conflicting things about him, how can we not marvel at such a nature, so plainly great in its gifts, setting its hand to great tasks, and possessing a boldness not to be lightly dismissed?

If one looked further into such a man’s life, how could one fail to ask how he, brought up in humble circumstances and poverty, having received no general education and having learned none of the arguments and doctrines that might have made him persuasive in addressing crowds, swaying the people and drawing more hearers, gave himself to teaching new doctrines? He brought the human race a teaching that set aside the customs of the Jews while still honouring their prophets, and that overthrew the laws of the Greeks, above all those concerning the divine. And how could such a man, brought up in this way, who had learned nothing of worth from any human being (as even those who speak evil of him admit), say such things about the judgment of God, about punishments for wickedness and honours for goodness, and say them in a way not easily despised, so that not only rustic and unlearned people were won by what he said, but also not a few of the more intelligent, those able to see into the hidden sense of sayings thought to be told in plain and humble words, a hidden sense that holds within it, so to speak, something more secret?

The man of Seriphus in Plato reproached Themistocles, who had become famous for his generalship, saying that he had won his fame not by his own character but by the good fortune of having the most celebrated fatherland in all Greece. He heard this reply from Themistocles, who was fair-minded and saw that his fatherland too had contributed to his fame: “If I had been a Seriphian, I would not have become so famous; nor would you, had you been fortunate enough to be born an Athenian, have become a Themistocles” (Plato, Republic 329e–330a). But our Jesus was reproached with coming from a village, and that not a Greek village, nor belonging to any nation held in esteem by most people. He was slandered as the son of a poor woman who worked with her hands, and as having left his fatherland because of poverty to work for hire in Egypt. To use the example already given, he was not only a Seriphian, from the smallest and most obscure of islands, but, so to speak, the most low-born of Seriphians. Yet he has been able to stir the whole inhabited world, more than Themistocles the Athenian, and more even than Pythagoras and Plato and any other wise men, kings or generals anywhere in the world.

choices.choice: The Seriphian anecdote is Plato, Republic 1.329e–330a (also told, with a man of Belbina, in Herodotus 8.125); Origen's wording of the reply differs from Plato's, so the quotation is translated as Origen gives it. Text: θανμαστέον read as θαυμαστέον; 'ἔθνους ἔθνους ὄντος' is a doubled word, read once. τὰ ἀνόμοια λεγούσῃ: the world 'saying conflicting things about him' (praise and blame); possibly 'saying things unlike [the facts]', but the first fits better. 'Those who speak evil of him admit' refers back to Celsus's Jew in 1.28. No Scripture quoted; 'set aside the customs of the Jews' is not taken as a clear allusion to Matthew 5:17. ἀπόκρυψις rendered 'hidden sense' rather than 'veil', to avoid importing the veil image of 2 Corinthians 3.
ἐμφανὴς καὶ δῆλος: 'famous and plain to see' -> 'conspicuous and well known'
τοιαῦτα ... λέγειν ... οὐκ εὐκαταφρονήτως: restored the omitted 'such things' ('say such things ... and say them in a way not easily despised')
ἀπόκρυψις: 'veil' (a metaphor not in the Greek) -> 'hidden sense'; εὐτελεστέρων ... ἀπαγγέλλεσθαι -> 'told in plain and humble words'
ἀκήκοεν ἀπὸ ... Θεμιστοκλέους: kept the Greek agency ('He heard this reply from Themistocles') instead of 'Themistocles answered'
καὶ ἡ πατρίς: 'had indeed contributed' -> 'too had contributed'
Checked Plato, Republic 329e–330a for the Seriphian story
